It has a very religious tone to it, except a major difference between it and let's say Christianity, is the fact that the whole belief system of the latter is based upon a higher power, the divine, God, who holds the world in His hands. The human surrendering of control, recognition of widespread sin and faith in God and His good works is at direct odds with what I understand underpins effective altruism - that is the ability for humans to be all knowing, directors of morality and judgement. I see it as a 21st century, technocrat-led alternative to traditional religions that won’t age well due to its reliance on the fallibility of human beings.

Putting religion and faith to the side, my experiences thus far in life have led me to believe that surrender and spirituality are foundational and deeply relieving - helping to exhaust fight against things you cannot control, reduce stress, accept reality and find inner peace. The key ingredient is that none of these things rest on human control; they are the direct opposite, a release of control to a different dimension if you will. When I think about the effective altruism movement and some of the characters at play, it’s not surprising to me to see the outcomes it has produced - hubris, greed and rapid rises paired with dramatic falls (eg SBF). These are all quintessentially human characteristics that everyone experiences (eg all humans are sinners), but they are not characteristics that God embodies (no matter who your God is).

While many might read this and ask why am I writing about it, I find the topic interesting from a personal perspective but oddly enough, it also carries relevance for markets. Crypto funding fell 58% in September.

Yet these 11 companies still raised almost $600M, with Nasdaq, Binance and S&P Global among the investors.

Here’s where the money went:

1. @Felixpago ($200M): A WhatsApp-based remittance platform. Probably the simplest idea here: let people send money internationally through an app they already use every day.

2. @Payward ($100M): Kraken's parent company raised from Nasdaq. Pretty interesting timing considering both companies are getting deeper into tokenized assets and 24/7 financial markets.

3. @circle ($100M): Binance invested directly into Circle.  That's an exchange buying a piece of the stablecoin infrastructure it already runs on, which is a different kind of bet than a VC check.

4. @kaikodata ($57M): Crypto market data for institutions. The interesting part is who backed it: S&P Global, alongside other major financial players.

5. @USDai_Official ($40M): A stablecoin/yield project built around financing AI infrastructure. Basically crypto capital being used to fund GPUs and compute.

6. @carinetwork ($32.5M): Building tokenized bank deposits. Instead of putting another stablecoin onchain, the idea is to bring actual bank deposits there.

7. @OpenReserveBank ($25M): Blockchain-native banking + stablecoin infrastructure, with a16z leading the round. So the crypto VCs haven't completely sat this out either.

Then underneath that:

- @dtcpay_official ($15M): stablecoin payments
- @tarecredit ($13.25M): private credit
- @velocityxyz_ ($10M): stablecoin payments + treasury
- @deadstock_app ($2.5M): onchain trading cards, which doesn't fit any theme here, but I liked it.

What stands out to me is who wrote the biggest checks.

Nasdaq, Binance and S&P Global don't need a 10x from these deals the way a VC does. To me it looks more like they're buying into infrastructure they want to use themselves.

That matters because VC money moves with the cycle, and this kind of money mostly doesn't. When funding falls off a cliff and these guys are still writing $100M checks, I read it more as them deciding this stuff is gonna be part of how finance actually runs.

Funding slowed, but the same themes kept getting checks: stablecoins, payments, tokenized assets, private credit, financial data.

So what it shows is who's still buying while everyone else cuts, and in September a lot of those buyers were TradFi names.

When we are in meetings, we use a tool for what we call "dotting." It allows everyone to convey what they are seeing and how each person is behaving in real time.
You can look at a screen and see, in color, how people are seeing each other. You see who thinks something is the most arrogant thing, or the stupidest thing, or that you aren't being considerate.

When you see that visualization in real time, you are forced to ask yourself: How do I know that I’m seeing it the right way? How do I know that I’m not the wrong one?
You realize you are just one of those dots in that line and in that grid. It causes you to go above yourself and provides perspective. Once you see how everyone else is seeing the situation, it raises a fundamental question: Together, how do we know what’s best?

Just because an idea is in your head doesn’t mean it’s best. To make the right decisions, we have to look past our own individual assumptions and work together to find the truth.

One of my frustrations building an AI startup at the application layer was this feeling that I was basically a token reseller.

You can have huge revenue, great retention, happy customers, all of it. But if a big chunk of every dollar goes straight to the model provider, you start wondering how much of the business you’re actually building for yourself.

And yes, you can use open source models. For some tasks they’re great, for others you still need the frontier. But even if you own the weights, you still need somewhere to run them.

Without scale, compute is expensive. Need a lot of it quickly? You pay another premium. Meanwhile the labs are locking in enormous amounts of capacity years ahead, with economics you probably can’t get as a startup.

So switching away from an API doesn’t magically solve the margin problem. You go from buying tokens to buying compute, and you’re still buying from someone with more scale and negotiating power than you.

That’s fine as long as you’re building something customers value enough to pay a healthy margin on top. It gets uncomfortable when your supplier starts competing with you. They can charge less for the same product and still make more money on each customer than you do.

In an ideal world, you want to own the weights without having to spend billions training the model yourself. That’s why open source is so awesome. You want to be able to switch models and providers without getting locked in, and run inference with a cloud provider that has the scale you don’t and actually passes those economies of scale on to you.

You don’t need to own everything. But you want the freedom to switch, and the economics to build a business that’s yours.
